{{No footnotes|date=September 2026}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Vitali–Hahn–Saks theorem''', introduced by  {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Giuseppe Vitali|last=Vitali|year=1907}}, {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Hans Hahn (mathematician)|last=Hahn|year=1922}}, and {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Stanisław Saks|last=Saks|year=1933}}, proves that a pointwise convergent sequence of finite [[Measure_(mathematics)|measures]] is uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to any common dominating finite measure, and its limit is also a finite measure. This holds in the more general setting of finite [[Signed measure|signed measures]] or [[Complex measure|complex measures]].

==Preliminaries==

Let <math>(S,\mathcal{B})</math> be a [[measurable space]] and let <math>\lambda</math> be a complex measure. The [[Total variation#Total variation norm of complex measures|variation]] of <math>\lambda</math> is the finite measure <math>|\lambda|\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathbb{R}</math> given by
<math display=block>
|\lambda|(B) = \sup_{\pi} \sum_{A\in\pi} |\lambda(A)|,
</math>
where the supremum is taken over all partitions <math>\pi</math> of <math>B</math> into a countable number of disjoint measurable subsets. The [[Total variation#Total variation norm of complex measures|total variation]] is then <math>\lVert\lambda\rVert_{TV} = |\lambda|(S)</math>.

A complex measure <math>\lambda</math> is called [[Absolute continuity of measures#Absolute continuity of measures|absolutely continuous]] with respect to some measure <math>m</math> (denoted <math>\lambda\ll m</math>), if <math>|\lambda|(B)=0</math> for all measurable sets <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math> with <math>m(B)=0</math>. This is equivalent to the following: For every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> there is a <math>\delta>0</math> so that <math>m(B)<\delta</math> implies <math>|\lambda|(B)<\varepsilon</math>. Since
<math display=block>
|\lambda(B)| \le |\lambda|(B) \le 4 \sup_{A\subseteq B} |\lambda(A)|,
</math>
absolute continuity is also equivalent to the following: For every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> there is a <math>\delta>0</math> so that <math>m(B)<\delta</math> implies <math>|\lambda(B)|<\varepsilon</math>.

If <math>\lambda\ll m</math>, then, by the [[Radon–Nikodym theorem]] there is an integrable function <math>f\colon S\to\mathbb{C}</math>, such that <math>\textstyle\lambda(B)=\int_B f \, dm</math> for every measurable <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math>. This function is uniquely defined up to an <math>m</math>-null set and called a Radon–Nikodym derivative of <math>\lambda</math> with respect to <math>m</math>. It is usually denoted by <math>\textstyle f = \frac{d\lambda}{dm}</math>.

==Statement of the theorem==

Let <math>(S,\mathcal{B})</math> be a [[measurable space]] and let <math>(\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> be a sequence of finite complex measures such that the pointwise limit <math>\textstyle\lim_{n\to\infty} \lambda_n(B)</math> exists in <math>\mathbb{C}</math> for every measurable set <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math>. Define the function <math>\lambda\colon\mathcal{B}\to\mathbb{C}</math> by
<math display=block>
\lambda(B) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \lambda_n(B).
</math>
Then, the following holds:
* Countable Additivity and Boundedness: <math>\lambda</math> is countably additive and thus a finite complex measure. Furthermore, <math>\sup_{n\ge1} \lVert\lambda_n\rVert_{TV} < \infty</math> and <math>\lVert\lambda\rVert_{TV} < \infty</math>.
* Absolute Continuity: Assume that <math>m</math> is a finite measure on <math>(S,\mathcal{B})</math> satisfying <math>\lambda_n\ll m</math> for all <math>n\ge1</math>, such as <math display=block>m=\sum_{n\ge1} \frac{|\lambda_n|}{2^n(1+\lVert\lambda_n\rVert_{TV})}\,.</math>Then, <math>\lambda</math> is also absolutely continuous with respect to <math>m</math>, that is <math>\lambda\ll m</math>, and the sequence <math>(\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> is uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to <math>m</math>, that is, for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> there is a <math>\delta>0</math> so that <math>m(B)<\delta</math> implies <math>|\lambda_n(B)|<\varepsilon</math> uniformly for all <math>n\ge1</math>.
* Densities: Again, if <math>m</math> is a finite measure on <math>(S,\mathcal{B})</math> satisfying <math>\lambda_n\ll m</math> for all <math>n\ge1</math>, set <math>\textstyle f_n = \frac{d\lambda_n}{dm}</math> for all <math>n\ge1</math> and <math>\textstyle f = \frac{d\lambda}{dm}</math>. Then, <math>(f_n)_{n\ge1}</math> is [[Uniform integrability|uniformly integrable]] and <math>f_n</math> converges in <math>L^1(S,\mathcal B,m)</math> with respect to the [[weak topology]] <math>\sigma(L^1,L^\infty)</math>, that is, <math display=block>\int g f_n \, dm \to \int g f \, dm</math> for all bounded measurable <math>g\colon S\to\mathbb{C}</math>.

==Preparations for the Proof==

Let <math>(S,\mathcal{B},m)</math> be a [[measure space]] and write <math>\mathcal{B}_0</math> to denote the set of measurable sets <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math> with <math>m(B)<\infty</math>:
<math display=block>
\mathcal{B}_0 = \{B\in\mathcal{B} : m(B)<\infty\}.
</math>
Write <math>B_1\mathbin\vartriangle B_2 = (B_1\setminus B_2) \cup (B_2\setminus B_1)</math> to denote the 
[[symmetric difference]] of the sets <math>B_1,B_2</math>. Define the [[equivalence relation]] <math>\approx</math> on <math>\mathcal{B}_0</math> by <math>B_1\approx B_2</math> if <math>m(B_1\mathbin\vartriangle B_2)=0</math>. Write <math>\bar\mathcal{B}_0 = \mathcal{B}_0/\mathord{\approx}</math> to denote the [[quotient set]] of <math>\mathcal{B}_0</math> with respect to the equivalence relation <math>\approx</math>:
<math display=block>
\bar\mathcal{B}_0 = \{ \bar B : B\in\mathcal{B}_0 \},
</math>
where <math>\bar B = \{ A\in\mathcal{B}_0 : A\approx B \}</math> is the equivalence class of <math>B</math>. Then, <math>m</math> induces a well-defined quotient map on <math>\bar\mathcal{B}_0</math> which is denoted by <math>\bar m</math>: <math>\bar m(\bar B)=m(B)</math>.

'''Proposition:''' Define <math>d_m\colon\bar\mathcal{B}_0\times\bar\mathcal{B}_0\to\mathbb{R}</math> by
<math display=block>
d_m(\bar B_1,\bar B_2) = m(B_1\mathbin\vartriangle B_2).
</math>
Then, <math>d_m</math> is well-defined and <math>(\bar\mathcal{B}_0,d_m)</math> is a [[complete metric space]].

{{Collapse top|title=Proof of the Proposition}}
Using [[Indicator function|indicator functions]] as before, we have
<math display=block>
d_m(\bar B_1,\bar B_2)
= m(B_1\mathbin\vartriangle B_2)
= \int |\mathbf1_{B_1}-\mathbf1_{B_2}| \, dm
= \lVert \mathbf1_{B_1}-\mathbf1_{B_2}\rVert_1.
</math>
This means that the metric space <math>(\bar\mathcal{B}_0,d_m)</math> can be identified with a subset of the [[Lp space|space]] <math>L^1(S,\mathcal{B},m)</math> which is a [[Banach space]]. Hence, <math>d_m</math> is a well-defined metric. Consider a [[Cauchy sequence]] <math>(\bar B_n)_{n\ge1}</math>. Then,
<math display=block>
\lim_{k,n\to\infty} d_m(\bar B_k,\bar B_n)
= \lim_{k,n\to\infty} \lVert\mathbf1_{B_k} - \mathbf1_{B_n}\rVert_1 = 0.
</math>
Hence, we can choose a subsequence <math>(\bar B_{n_k})_{k\ge1}</math> such that
<math>(\mathbf1_{B_{n_k}})_{k\ge1}</math> converges [[almost everywhere]]. Define <math>g\colon S\to\mathbb{R}</math> by
<math display=block>
g(x) = \lim_{k\to\infty} \mathbf1_{B_{n_k}}.
</math>
Then, <math>g</math> is measurable, has values in <math>\{0,1\}</math> almost everywhere and
<math display=block>
\lim_{k\to\infty} \lVert\mathbf1_{B_{n_k}} - g\rVert_1 = 0.
</math>
Therefore, <math>g = \mathbf1_{B_{\infty}}</math> almost everywhere for some <math>B_{\infty}\in\mathcal{B}_0</math> and
<math display=block>
\lim_{k\to\infty} d_m(\bar B_{n_k}, \bar B_\infty)
= \lim_{k\to\infty} \lVert\mathbf1_{B_{n_k}} - \mathbf1_{B_\infty}\rVert_1 = 0,
</math>
that is, the Cauchy sequence <math>(\bar B_n)_{n\ge1}</math> contains a convergent subsequence and is convergent itself. Therefore, <math>\bar\mathcal{B}_0</math> is complete. We remark that <math>B_{\infty}</math> is explicitly given by the [[limit inferior]] of the sequence <math>(\bar B_{n_k})_{k\ge1}</math>:
<math display=block>
B_\infty
= \liminf_{k\to\infty} B_{n_k}
= \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty \bigcap_{j=k}^\infty B_{n_j}.
</math>
{{Collapse bottom}}


'''Proposition:''' Let <math>(\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> be a sequence of complex measures such that <math>(\lVert\lambda_n\rVert_{TV})_{n\ge1}</math> is bounded. Then, <math>(\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> converges pointwise, that is, the sequence <math>(\lambda_n(B))_{n\ge1}</math> converges for every <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math>, if and only if, for every bounded measurable function <math>g\colon S\to\mathbb{C}</math>, the sequence
<math>\textstyle(\int g \, d\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math>
converges.

{{Collapse top|title=Proof of the Proposition}}
The implication <math>\Leftarrow</math> is obvious, since, for every <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math>, the [[indicator function]] <math>\mathbf 1_B</math> with
<math display=block>
\mathbf 1_B(x) = \begin{cases}
   1, & \text{if } x\in B, \\
   0, & \text{if } x\notin B,
\end{cases}
</math>
is bounded and measurable and <math>\textstyle\lambda_n(B) = \int \mathbf 1_B \, d\lambda_n</math>. For the other implication <math>\Rightarrow</math>, we first note that, by linearity of limits, the sequence <math>\textstyle(\int s \, d\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> converges for all measurable [[Simple function|simple functions]] <math>s\colon S\to\mathbb{C}</math>. Write <math>K</math> for the bound of total variations:
<math display=block>
K = \sup_{n\ge1} \lVert\lambda_n\rVert_{TV}.
</math>
Given a bounded measurable function <math>g\colon S\to\mathbb{C}</math> and an <math>\varepsilon>0</math> there is a measurable simple function <math>s\colon S\to\mathbb{C}</math> with <math>\lVert g-s\rVert_\infty<\varepsilon</math>. Furthermore, <math>\textstyle(\int s \, d\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> converges, thus there exists <math>N</math> such that
<math display=block>
\left| \int s \, d\lambda_k - \int s \, d\lambda_n \right| < \varepsilon
</math>
for all <math>k,n>N</math>. Then,
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
\left| \int g \, d\lambda_k - \int g \, d\lambda_n \right|
&\le \left| \int g \, d\lambda_k - \int s \, d\lambda_k \right| + \left| \int s \, d\lambda_k - \int s \, d\lambda_n \right| + \left| \int s \, d\lambda_n - \int g \, d\lambda_n \right| \\
&\le \int |g-s| \, d|\lambda_k| + \left| \int s \, d\lambda_k - \int s \, d\lambda_n \right| + \int |g-s| \, d|\lambda_n| \\
&< \varepsilon (2K+1)
\end{align}
</math>
for all <math>k,n>N</math>. Consequently, the sequence <math>\textstyle(\int g \, d\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> converges.
{{Collapse bottom}}


Let <math>m</math> be a measure on <math>(S,\mathcal{B})</math>. Fix some <math>\delta>0</math>. A set <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math> is called <math>\delta</math>-indivisible, if it cannot be partitioned into two disjoint measurable subsets <math>B_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}</math> satisfying <math>m(B_1)\ge\delta</math> and <math>m(B_2)\ge\delta</math>.

'''Proposition:''' Let <math>m</math> be a finite measure on <math>(S,\mathcal{B})</math> and fix some <math>\delta>0</math>. Then, there exists a partition <math>\pi</math> of <math>S</math> into at most <math>\lfloor m(S)/\delta\rfloor+1</math> disjoint <math>\delta</math>-indivisible, measurable sets.

{{Collapse top|title=Proof of the Proposition}}
Start with the partition <math>\pi_1=\{S\}</math>. Assume that <math>\pi_n</math> is already defined. If all sets in <math>\pi_n</math> are already <math>\delta</math>-indivisible, then set <math>\pi_{n+1}=\pi_n</math>. If not, pick one set <math>B\in\pi_n</math> that is not <math>\delta</math>-indivisible. Then, <math>B</math> can be partitioned into two disjoint measurable subsets <math>B_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}</math> satisfying <math>m(B_1)\ge\delta</math> and <math>m(B_2)\ge\delta</math>. In this case, set <math>\pi_{n+1} = (\pi_n \setminus \{B\}) \cup \{B_1, B_2\}</math>. This process must stabilize after at most <math>\lfloor m(S)/\delta\rfloor</math>, since each splitting creates a new set of measure at least <math>\delta</math>.
{{Collapse bottom}}


==Proof of Vitali-Hahn-Saks theorem==

Let <math>m</math> be a finite measure on <math>(S,\mathcal{B})</math> satisfying <math>\lambda_n\ll m</math> for all <math>n\ge1</math>. If none is given, take for instance
<math display=block>
m = \sum_{n\ge1} \frac{|\lambda_n|}{2^n(1+\lVert\lambda_n\rVert_{TV})}\,,
</math>
as mentioned above. Since <math>m</math> is finite, we have <math>\mathcal{B}_0 = \mathcal{B}</math>. Furthermore, we write <math>\bar\mathcal{B}</math> for the quotient set <math>\bar\mathcal{B}_0</math> above. Each <math>\lambda_n</math> defines a quotient map <math>\bar\lambda_n</math> on <math>\bar\mathcal{B}</math> by <math>\bar\lambda_n(\bar B)=\lambda_n(B)</math>. This quotient map <math>\bar\lambda_n</math> is well-defined: If <math>A\in\bar B</math>, then <math>m(A\mathbin\vartriangle B)=0</math> and thus <math>|\lambda_n|(A\mathbin\vartriangle B)=0</math>, since <math>\lambda_n\ll m</math>. Therefore, <math>\lambda_n(A)=\lambda_n(B)</math>. Moreover, <math>\bar\lambda_n</math> is continuous as a function from the metric space <math>(\bar\mathcal{B},d_m)</math> to <math>\mathbb C</math>.

Fix <math>\varepsilon>0</math>. For every <math>n,k\ge1</math> the function <math>|\bar\lambda_n - \bar\lambda_{n+k}|</math> is again continuous, so that
<math display=block>
F_{n,k,\varepsilon}
= \left\{ \bar B\in\bar\mathcal{B} \,:\,
    |\bar\lambda_n(\bar B) - \bar\lambda_{n+k}(\bar B)|
         \le \varepsilon \right\}
</math>
is a closed subset of <math>\bar\mathcal{B}</math>. Consequently,
<math display=block>
F_{n,\varepsilon}
= \bigcap_{k\ge1} F_{n,k,\varepsilon}
= \left\{ \bar B\in\bar\mathcal{B} \,:\,
    \sup_{k\ge1} |\bar\lambda_n(\bar B) - \bar\lambda_{n+k}(\bar B)|
         \le \varepsilon \right\}
</math>
is also a closed subset of <math>\bar\mathcal{B}</math>. By the hypothesis the sequence <math>(\lambda_n(B))_{n\ge1}</math> converges for every <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math>, so that
<math display=block>
\sup_{k\ge1} |\bar\lambda_n(\bar B) - \bar\lambda_{n+k}(\bar B)|
= \sup_{k\ge1} |\lambda_n(B) - \lambda_{n+k}(B)|
\to 0.
</math>
Therefore, we obtain
<math display=block>
\bar\mathcal{B} = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty F_{n,\varepsilon}.
</math>
By [[Baire category theorem]] at least one of the sets <math>(F_{n,\varepsilon})_{n\ge1}</math> must contain a non-empty open set of <math>\bar\mathcal{B}</math>. This means that there is <math>n_0\ge1</math> and <math>B_0\in\mathcal{B}</math> and an <math>r_0>0</math> such that <math>F_{n_0,\varepsilon}</math> contains the open ball in <math>\bar\mathcal{B}</math> with center <math>\bar B_0</math> and radius <math>r_0</math>:
<math display=block>
\{ \bar B\in\bar\mathcal B : d_m(\bar B,\bar B_0)<r_0 \}
\subseteq F_{n_0,\varepsilon}.
</math>
In other words:
<math display=block>
d_m(\bar B,\bar B_0)<r_0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sup_{k\geq1} |\bar\lambda_{n_0}(\bar B)-\bar\lambda_{n_0+k}(\bar B)|
\le\varepsilon.
</math>
Since <math>\lambda_n\ll m</math> for all <math>n<n_0</math>, there is a <math>\delta>0</math>, so that <math>m(B)<\delta</math> implies <math>|\lambda_n(B)|<\varepsilon</math> for all <math>n<n_0</math>. We may choose <math>\delta>0</math> sufficiently small, so that <math>\delta\le r_0</math>.

Now, consider a measurable set <math>B\in\mathcal{B}</math> with <math>m(B)<\delta</math>. Define <math>B_1=B\cup B_0</math> and <math>B_2=B_0\setminus B</math>. Then, we have
<math display=block>
B
= (B\cup B_0) \setminus (B_0\setminus B) 
= B_1 \setminus B_2
</math>
and
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
d_m(\bar B_1, \bar B_0)
&= m(B_1 \mathbin\vartriangle B_0)
= m((B\cup B_0) \mathbin\vartriangle B_0)
\le m(B)
< \delta, \\
d_m(\bar B_2, \bar B_0)
&= m(B_2 \mathbin\vartriangle B_0)
= m((B_0\setminus B) \mathbin\vartriangle B_0)
\le m(B)
< \delta.
\end{align}
</math>
Thus, if <math>n<n_0</math>, then <math>|\lambda_n(B)|<\varepsilon</math> and, if <math>n\ge n_0</math>, then
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
|\lambda_n(B)|
&\le |\lambda_{n_0}(B)| + |\lambda_{n_0}(B)-\lambda_n(B)| \\
&\le |\lambda_{n_0}(B)| + |\lambda_{n_0}(B_1)-\lambda_n(B_1)| + |\lambda_{n_0}(B_2)-\lambda_n(B_2)| \\
&< 3\epsilon
\end{align}
</math>
Therefore, <math>(\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> is uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to <math>m</math>.

By the linearity of the limit <math>\lambda</math> is [[Sigma_additivity#Additive_(or_finitely_additive)_set_functions|finitely additive]]. And by uniformly absolute continuity of <math>(\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> the limit <math>\lambda</math> is actually countably additive.

Next, we prove boundedness of the total variations: Fix <math>\varepsilon=1</math>. By uniformly absolute continuity of <math>(\lambda_n)_{n\ge1}</math> there is <math>\delta>0</math> such that <math>m(B)<\delta</math> implies <math>|\lambda_n(B)|<1</math>. By the third proposition above, there is a finite partition <math>\pi</math> of <math>S</math> into <math>\delta</math>-indivisible sets with respect to the finite measure <math>m</math>. For any <math>B\in\pi</math> and any measurable <math>A\subseteq B</math>, we cannot have both, <math>m(A)\ge\delta</math> and <math>m(B\setminus A)\ge\delta</math>. If <math>m(A)<\delta</math>, then, by uniformly absolute continuity,
<math display=block>
|\lambda_n(A)| < 1 \le |\lambda_n(B)|+1
</math>
for all <math>n\ge1</math>. If, on the other hand <math>m(B\setminus A)<\delta</math>, then, again by uniform absolute continuity, <math>|\lambda_n(B\setminus A)|<1</math> for all <math>n\ge1</math>, which implies
<math display=block>
|\lambda_n(A)|
=|\lambda_n(B)-\lambda_n(B\setminus A)|
\le |\lambda_n(B)|+|\lambda_n(B\setminus A)|
< |\lambda_n(B)|+1
</math>
for all <math>n\ge1</math>. In both cases, for every measurable subset <math>A\subseteq B</math> and every <math>n\ge1</math>:
<math display=block>
|\lambda_n(A)| < |\lambda_n(B)|+1
</math>
Thus,
<math display=block>
|\lambda_n|(B)
\le 4 \sup_{A\subseteq B} |\lambda_n(A)|
\le 4 |\lambda_n(B)| + 4
</math>
Since <math>(\lambda_n(B))_{n\ge1}</math> converges for every <math>B\in\pi</math> and <math>\pi</math> is finite, we have
<math display=block>
C = \max_{B\in\pi} \sup_{n\ge1} |\lambda_n(B)| < \infty
</math>
and therefore
<math display=block>
\lVert\lambda_n\rVert_{TV}
= \sum_{B\in\pi} |\lambda_n|(B)
\le \sum_{B\in\pi} (4|\lambda_n(B)|+4)
\le (4C+4)|\pi| < \infty.
</math>

The remaining assertions of the theorem follow directly using the second proposition above and boundedness of all total variations.
